### NIMBYism: What the Record Shows About the Veto Over Housing, Energy, and Data Centers

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-13T19:45:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-13-nimby-record.html

Special Report

Concrete · Cement · Rome · The Concrete Club · Carbon · John Wilson

Objective

NIMBYism: What the Record Shows About the Veto Over Housing, Energy, and Data Centers

Support for housing, clean energy, data centers, and homeless services runs high in the abstract and collapses at specific addresses, in every ideology and tenure, for reasons the research literature has now measured: losses weigh roughly twice gains, a home is an undiversifiable asset, developer profit alone raises opposition by twenty points, and the hearings that decide hear almost only from opponents.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1945 ET, Friday, November 13, 2026.

The opposition has a consistent structure across fifty years of American land-use fights, and the research literature now describes it with unusual precision. Residents support housing, clean energy, data centers, and homeless services in the abstract at high rates. They oppose the same facilities at specific addresses near their homes at high rates. The gap between the two positions is not explained by ideology: renters in expensive cities register it at nearly the same level as homeowners, and liberal homeowners register it alongside conservatives. Three mechanisms account for most of the measured effect. Losses register roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains. A home is most owners' largest asset and cannot be diversified, so its protection dominates local voting. And opposition rises measurably when a developer's profit is made salient, by twenty percentage points in the best-known experiment, an effect its authors attribute to resentment of the developer's gain rather than fear of the resident's loss. The venues that decide these questions hear almost exclusively from opponents: in the largest study of hearing participation, about two-thirds of commenters opposed the housing before them and about fifteen percent supported it. The outcomes are legible in the record: a 495-home project on a San Francisco parking lot reversed on environmental grounds in 2021 and still unbuilt in 2026; a 25,000-job Amazon campus withdrawn from Queens in 2019 while polls showed most New Yorkers approved of it; data-center projects worth $130 billion blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026 alone.

The gap, measured

Michael Hankinson's study of San Francisco's 2015 election and a national survey, published in the American Political Science Review in 2018, found that renters in high-rent cities express opposition to market-rate housing near them at a level similar to homeowners, while simultaneously supporting large increases in their city's overall housing supply. Hankinson calls the preferences scale-dependent: support at the scale of the city, opposition at the scale of the street. William Marble and Clayton Nall, in the Journal of Politics, found the same split running through ideology. Liberal homeowners, in their title's phrase, are where "self-interest trumps ideology": they endorse egalitarian and redistributive housing policies in principle and oppose dense housing development in their own communities, with homeownership predicting local opposition more reliably than party or professed belief. New York City's 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey supplies the context in which these preferences operate: a net rental vacancy rate of 1.41 percent, the lowest since the survey began in 1968, with roughly 33,000 units available for rent in a city of 8.3 million.

The mechanisms in the literature

Prospect theory, the framework Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published in 1979 and extended in 1992, estimates that losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains; their 1992 estimate of the loss-aversion coefficient was 2.25, and later meta-analyses center somewhat lower without disturbing the asymmetry. Applied to a development proposal, the accounting is structural: the costs, construction, traffic, shadow, change itself, are immediate, visible, and assigned to identifiable households, while the benefits, marginally lower regional rents, a larger tax base, grid capacity, are delayed and divided among millions. William Fischel's homevoter hypothesis, set out in his 2001 book of that name, adds the balance sheet. For most owners the home is by far their largest financial asset; unlike stockholders they cannot diversify it across communities, and Fischel argues that fear of a capital loss turns owners into systematic voters for whatever protects the asset, including restrictions on nearby density. The third mechanism is the least comfortable. Paavo Monkkonen and Michael Manville of UCLA ran a survey experiment with more than 1,300 Los Angeles County respondents and found that telling respondents a developer would earn a large profit raised opposition to a housing project by twenty percentage points, double the increase produced by a traffic warning and comparable to the neighborhood-character warning. Their published conclusion: "some opposition to housing is motivated not by residents' fears of their own losses, but resentment of others' gains." Opposition, in the experiment, could be purchased by framing alone, without changing anything about the project.

The venue

Katherine Levine Einstein, David Glick, and Maxwell Palmer coded thousands of comments from planning and zoning hearings across 97 Massachusetts communities for their 2019 book Neighborhood Defenders. The people who speak are not a cross-section of the public. They are disproportionately older, whiter, more male, and longer-tenured than their communities, and they are far more likely to own their homes; about 41 percent lived on the same block as the proposed project. Roughly two-thirds of commenters opposed the housing under consideration; about fifteen percent spoke in favor. The people who would occupy unbuilt housing have no standing in this venue: they do not yet live in the jurisdiction, and many do not know the hearing exists. In California, the environmental-review statute supplies a second venue. A September 2026 Holland & Knight study of 498 appellate decisions under the California Environmental Quality Act found that housing was the largest single category of appealed project, at 25.5 percent of decisions; about 90 percent of the challenged housing projects were infill; project approvals ultimately prevailed in 75 percent of the decisions, after the delay the litigation imposed; and earlier analyses by the same firm found that suits filed in 2020 alone challenged roughly 48,000 approved housing units, and that only 13 percent of CEQA lawsuits were brought by anyone with a prior record of environmental advocacy. In 2025 the California legislature exempted most urban infill housing from CEQA review, a statutory concession that the channel had become a general-purpose instrument of delay.

Case file: a parking lot in San Francisco

At 469 Stevenson Street in San Francisco, a developer proposed a 27-story building with 495 rental homes, 73 of them affordable, on a 28,790-square-foot surface parking lot holding 176 cars. The Planning Commission certified the project's environmental impact report on July 29, 2021. On appeal by a neighborhood consortium, the Board of Supervisors voted 8 to 3 on October 26, 2021 to reverse the certification and require further study, citing, among other things, gentrification and geotechnical questions, on a site that was a parking lot. The state housing department warned the rejection risked violating the Housing Accountability Act. A partially recirculated report followed; the project was re-approved in 2023, into a high-interest-rate construction market. As of 2026, nine years after the project was first proposed, the site remains a surface parking lot and no homes have been built.

Case file: Amazon in Queens

On November 13, 2018, Amazon announced it would split its second headquarters between Arlington, Virginia, and Long Island City, Queens: 25,000 jobs and $2.5 billion of investment at each site. New York's package comprised $1.525 billion in performance-based state incentives, including up to $1.2 billion in job-linked tax credits and a $505 million capital grant; with city tax benefits the total was universally reported as roughly $3 billion, most of it contingent tax relief on activity that had not yet occurred rather than cash in hand. Opposition organized immediately, led by state and city officials and by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whose district borders Long Island City, on grounds that included the subsidies, the secrecy of the negotiation, and Amazon's labor practices. Polling cut against the opposition's premise and for its strongest argument simultaneously: Quinnipiac found New York City voters approved of the deal 57 to 26 percent, while splitting 46 to 44 on the incentive package itself; Siena found 56 percent of state voters approved even with the incentives stated. On February 14, 2019, Amazon withdrew, citing the opposition of state and local politicians, and quoted a 70 percent support figure that matches neither published poll. Ocasio-Cortez, celebrating the withdrawal the same day, said: "if we were willing to give away $3 billion for this deal, we could invest those $3 billion in our district ourselves if we wanted to," naming teachers and subway repairs. The statement treated contingent tax relief as a spendable fund, which, as critics across the spectrum noted at the time, it was not. The aftermath is on the record: the centerpiece city-owned site, a Department of Education warehouse at 44-36 Vernon Boulevard, remained in that use for roughly six years; in February 2025 the city issued a request for expressions of interest to redevelop it. Amazon, for its part, expanded in Manhattan instead, leasing office space at Hudson Yards and hiring thousands of employees in New York without a headquarters campus or the Queens incentives.

The complication: data centers

The data-center fights of the last three years follow the same geometry, concentrated costs against diffuse benefits, but the local benefit side of the ledger is genuinely thinner, and the record supports part of the opposition's case. Virginia's Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, in its December 2024 study of the world's largest data-center market, reported industry figures of approximately 50 full-time permanent workers, about half of them contractors, at a typical 250,000-square-foot facility, against roughly 1,500 workers on site at peak construction. The fiscal side runs the other way: in the five Virginia localities with mature markets, data-center revenue supplied from under 1 percent to 31 percent of total local revenue in fiscal 2023, the 31 percent in Loudoun County. The resource side is the opposition's strongest ground: data centers consumed 26 percent of Virginia's electricity sales in 2023, and the commission's independent forecast found that unconstrained demand would double the state's total power demand within about a decade. Nationally, Data Center Watch, the tracking project whose figures Bloomberg and the banks cite, counted projects worth $130 billion blocked or delayed amid local opposition in the first quarter of 2026 alone, with at least $156 billion across 2025; the project's period figures overlap and are not additive. Opposition groups numbered more than 800 across 49 states by early 2026.

The complication: shelters and supportive housing

The facilities most often opposed on predicted-harm grounds have the most direct evidence available, and it runs against the predictions. The NYU Furman Center's study of New York City supportive housing found that property values within 500 feet of the developments dipped modestly during construction and then rose steadily after opening, performing no worse than comparable properties elsewhere. A 2026 working paper by Brown, Amoah, and co-authors found the temporal structure of the opposition itself: voters living 100 to 300 meters from newly opened homeless facilities became more supportive of homelessness spending after the facilities opened. The opposition, in their phrase, is "more prospective than retrospective": it is strongest before the facility exists and weakens on contact with it.

The responses on the record

Three bodies of evidence describe what happens when the veto is overridden or removed. Evan Mast's moving-chain research, published in the Journal of Urban Economics in 2023, traced some 52,000 residents of new market-rate buildings through six rounds of moves: building 100 new market-rate units leads 45 to 70 people to move out of below-median-income neighborhoods within about five years, as each vacated unit opens for the next household. Asquith, Mast, and Reed, in the Review of Economics and Statistics, found that large new apartment buildings in low-income areas lower rents within a few hundred meters by 5 to 7 percent relative to comparable areas farther away. At the scale of a whole city, Auckland's 2016 Unitary Plan upzoned roughly three-quarters of the city's residential land; a synthetic-control study by Greenaway-McGrevy and So found that eight years after the reform, Auckland rents were about 23 percent lower than the no-reform counterfactual, alongside a documented construction boom. New York's City of Yes, adopted December 5, 2024, is the American test now running: the Department of City Planning projects it will enable 82,000 homes over fifteen years, a projection of permitted capacity rather than of completed buildings.

What the record does not show

No study in this literature measures hypocrisy, and none needs to. The findings are consistent with sincere holders of every position involved: the loss-aversion asymmetry is a property of human cognition, the homevoter's incentive is rational given the asset, the hearing skew is a property of who can attend a weeknight meeting, and the spite component, though measured, accounts for a share of opposition rather than its whole. What the record shows is a system in which each of those individually comprehensible forces points the same way, toward refusal, and in which the beneficiaries of building, future residents, future employees, future taxpayers, are structurally absent from every room where the decision is made. The outcomes are therefore not a mystery requiring a theory of bad faith. They are the arithmetic of the rooms.

Mr. Witkoff said the next round is on the schedule but gave no date or place; the envoys will speak to Moscow again before Presidents Putin and Trump meet at APEC in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19.

### Concrete: What the Record Shows About the Most Consumed Material on Earth

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-13T18:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-13-concrete-record.html

Special Report

Concrete · Cement · Rome · The Concrete Club · Carbon · John Wilson

Objective

Concrete: What the Record Shows About the Most Consumed Material on Earth

Humanity makes about 30 billion tonnes of concrete a year, more of it than of any substance except water itself, and nearly everything it builds stands on a material most people cannot define: cement is an ingredient, not the material; the rock hardens by chemistry, not by drying; it is immensely strong pressed and weak pulled, which is why steel runs through it. This report prints what the record supports about the material, from the Roman mix that heals its own cracks, proven in a frozen Pompeii construction yard in December 2025, to the cartel that taxed New York's pours at two percent, to the carbon ledger that no clean power source can settle, because most of the emissions are the chemistry itself.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Friday, November 13, 2026.

The File in Brief

Concrete is a manufactured rock with a twenty-century documentary record, and the record supports a short set of load-bearing facts. The material is cement paste (Portland cement and water) binding sand and stone; it sets by hydration, a chemical reaction that proceeds underwater and continues for years, reaching about 90 percent of its strength in 28 days; its tensile strength runs a tenth to a seventh of its compressive strength, so modern concrete is a composite with steel, the steel carrying tension and the rock carrying compression. The Romans built with a volcanic-ash version, opus caementicium, whose durability was a mystery for two millennia; the mechanism, hot mixing with quicklime, leaving reactive lime clasts that dissolve into cracks and recrystallize as stone, was demonstrated by MIT researchers in Science Advances in January 2023 and confirmed archaeologically on December 9, 2025, when a Nature Communications paper reported an unfinished Pompeii construction site holding dry piles of quicklime premixed with pozzolan, exactly as the hypothesis required. The Pantheon, completed about 126 AD, remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. The modern material dates to Joseph Aspdin's 1824 patent for Portland cement and to the reinforced patents of the later nineteenth century, Monier's pivotal 1867 filing among them, and its monument is the Hoover Dam: 3.25 million cubic yards in the dam itself, by the Bureau of Reclamation's own figures, cooled through 582 miles of embedded pipe because a single monolithic pour would have taken an estimated 125 years to cool. The scale today is about 4 billion tonnes of cement a year, a figure now falling from its 2023 peak of 4.1 billion as China's building boom ends, and China poured more cement in 2011 to 2013, about 6.5 billion tonnes, than the United States poured in the entire twentieth century, about 4.5 billion. The costs are two. Cement accounts for 7 to 8 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and roughly 60 percent of that is process emissions from calcining limestone, chemistry rather than fuel, which is why the working fixes are clinker substitution, commercial since 2025 in the form of LC3, and carbon capture, operating since June 2025 at Heidelberg's Brevik plant in Norway; the third announced fix, electrochemical cement, has a standards designation and two technology-company offtake deals and no plant, its federal grant cancelled in May 2025 and its first works unbuilt toward 2028. And the material's American folklore is adjudicated fact: in 1980s New York, a club of six concrete contractors, coordinated by four crime families, controlled Manhattan contracts above $2 million and paid a 2 percent cut to Ralph Scopo, the concrete workers' union president who received 100 years in the 1986 Mafia Commission Trial. The culture keeps returning to the material, most recently John Wilson's 2026 feature documentary, The History of Concrete, and the desk's standard for the subject remains the one set by David Owen's 2003 New Yorker piece, whose famous figures this report prints as Owen's, where no primary source carries them.

The desk's method is the paper's method. Material was supplied to the desk as AI-assistant summaries of the literature and of The New Yorker's concrete file. Every checkable claim was re-verified against the primary record: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries read directly, the Science Advances and Nature Communications papers, the Second Circuit's opinion in United States v. Scopo, the Bureau of Reclamation's figures, ASTM's standards history, and the magazine's own archive for claims about the magazine. The supplied material was sound in outline and wrong in several load-bearing places, including the authorship of one of the magazine's best-known concrete pieces; the corrections are printed where they belong.

1. The Chemistry: It Does Not Dry

The first fact is a correction most adults carry uncorrected for life: cement and concrete are different things, and concrete does not harden by drying. Cement is a powder, an ingredient. Concrete is the composite: cement paste, sand, coarse aggregate such as gravel or crushed stone, and water, in proportions the engineer chooses. When water meets cement, the two react chemically, a process called hydration, forming calcium silicate hydrates, interlocking crystals that bind the aggregate into artificial stone. Because the hardening is a reaction and not an evaporation, hydraulic cement sets and gains strength underwater by definition, and pours are kept wet deliberately after placement to feed the reaction. Strength accrues on a curve: roughly 90 percent of design strength by 28 days, and, while moisture remains available, for years beyond it. David Owen's 2003 New Yorker piece, “Concrete Jungle,” opened its technical account on exactly this point, and on this point the textbooks and the magazine agree without reservation.

The second fact explains the steel. Concrete's compressive strength, its resistance to being crushed, is enormous and engineerable, from ordinary structural grades to the ultra-high-performance mixes Owen cited at up to 40,000 pounds per square inch, a figure the desk prints as Owen's; laboratory ultra-high-performance work reaches such strengths, and no primary source carries his number as a general claim. Its tensile strength, resistance to being pulled apart, runs only 10 to 15 percent of the compressive figure. A beam of plain concrete is strong stood upon and weak bent. The solution, patented into a system in the nineteenth century, is reinforcement: steel bars embedded in the wet mix where tension will run, so the finished member is two materials doing the two jobs, steel in tension, stone in compression. Nearly everything called concrete in the modern built world is that composite. The third fact is the clock. Wet concrete is perishable: the standard governing ready-mix, ASTM C94, required discharge within an hour and a half of mixing from 1935 until its 2021 revision left the limit to agreement between buyer and producer. Owen's roughly 90 minutes was not atmosphere; it was the specification of his era, and it is the fact on which the crime story in section 5 turns, because a perishable material delivered by truck is a material whose supply can be squeezed.

2. Rome: The Mix That Heals Itself

The oldest concrete in continuous service is Roman, and until recently nobody could say precisely why it lasts. Roman builders mixed lime with pozzolana, volcanic ash from the Pozzuoli region, to make opus caementicium, and built harbors that set in seawater and the Pantheon, completed about 126 AD under Hadrian, whose dome spans 43.3 meters, a diameter equal to the height from floor to oculus, and which remains, nineteen centuries later, the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth. The received account credited the ash. In January 2023, a team led by Admir Masic at MIT published the mechanism in Science Advances: Roman mortar was hot-mixed, combined with quicklime at high temperature, which left millimeter-scale lime clasts distributed through the material. The clasts were long read as evidence of sloppy mixing. They are the repair system. Cracks route preferentially through the brittle clasts; water entering a crack dissolves the lime, and the saturated solution recrystallizes as calcium carbonate, sealing the crack. In the laboratory, cracked Roman-style samples healed and stopped water flow within about two weeks, and modern-style samples did not.

In December 2025 the hypothesis stopped being a hypothesis. On December 9, Nature Communications published the analysis of an unfinished construction site in Pompeii's Regio IX, a house mid-renovation when Vesuvius froze it in 79 AD: dry piles of quicklime premixed with dry pozzolan, stored as ingredients, ready for hot mixing on the spot. The paper's word is “unequivocal,” and it contradicts the surviving Roman text, Vitruvius, whose account describes slaked lime prepared first. The builders' practice, it turns out, was better than the builders' literature. The desk prints the sequence because it is the cleanest science story in this file: a two-thousand-year-old durability observed, a mechanism proposed from microscopy in 2023, and the mechanism confirmed in the ground in 2025 by a construction yard that never got to pour. Modern concrete is stronger, faster, and reproducible to specification in a way Rome never approached; on the single axis of surviving its own cracks, the record now shows the Roman mix doing something the modern one does not, and shows why.

3. The Reinvention, the Dam, and the Scale of the Present Pour

Modern concrete is a nineteenth-century reinvention with named inventors and dated patents. In 1824, the English bricklayer Joseph Aspdin took British Patent 5022 for a cement he named Portland, a quality claim, not a place of manufacture: the product resembled the prized building stone of the Isle of Portland. Reinforcement followed within a generation; the desk prints the full line because the pastes do not: Joseph-Louis Lambot built a reinforced boat in 1848 and patented it in 1855, William Wilkinson patented reinforced floors in 1854, and Joseph Monier's 1867 patent, for large flowerpots strengthened with a cage of iron wires, became the pivotal filing from which the reinforced-concrete industry grew. François Hennebique patented his complete building system in 1892. Its American monument is the Hoover Dam, and the Bureau of Reclamation's own figures are the record: 3.25 million cubic yards of concrete in the dam, 4.36 million in the whole project, placed between June 6, 1933, and May 29, 1935. The dam could not be poured as one mass, because hydration is exothermic and a monolith of that size would, on Reclamation's estimate, have needed about 125 years to cool; it was built in blocks, with more than 582 miles of one-inch steel pipe embedded through them, circulating ice water from a plant making 1,000 tons of ice a day, the cooling finished in March 1935.

The Scale Ledger: Cement and Concrete, by the Record

MeasureFigureSource
World cement production, 20234.1 billion tonnesUSGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025
World cement production, 2024 (est.)4.0 billion tonnesUSGS MCS 2025
World cement production, 2025 (est.)&asymp;3.8 billion tonnes, China &asymp;1.7–1.8USGS MCS 2026, as reported
Concrete produced annually&asymp;30 billion tonnes (&asymp;14 billion m&sup3; in 2020)Gagg (2014); Global Cement and Concrete Association
China's cement use, 2011–2013&asymp;6.4–6.6 billion tonnesSmil, from USGS data
US cement use, entire 20th century&asymp;4.4–4.5 billion tonnesSmil / USGS (van Oss)
Sand and aggregate extracted annually40–50 billion tonnesUN Environment Programme, 2022 and 2026 reports

The standing summary, carried by the industry association and the literature, is that concrete is the second most consumed substance on Earth after water. The direction of the cement line has turned: the 4.1-billion-tonne figure repeated in most summaries is 2023's, and the world total has fallen since as China's construction boom contracts.

The China comparison survives verification and deserves its exact form. Vaclav Smil, working from USGS data, calculated that China used roughly 6.4 to 6.6 billion tonnes of cement in the three years 2011 to 2013, against roughly 4.4 to 4.5 billion tonnes for the United States across the whole twentieth century; the USGS's own cement specialist, Hendrik van Oss, put the comparison to the Washington Post in 2015 as China's 2010–12 consumption running at about 140 percent of America's 1900–99 total. It is the single most informative statistic in the modern material record: more cement in three years of one country's building boom than in the century that built the American dams, highways, and skylines combined. The same literature raises the sand question, and the desk prints both bearings on it. The UN Environment Programme reports 40 to 50 billion tonnes of sand and gravel extracted a year, calls sand the second most used resource after water, and documents real damage to rivers and coasts from unregulated extraction, most recently in its third sand report of May 2026. The USGS position runs beside it: sand and gravel are geologically plentiful, and what is scarce is cheap, angular, washed construction sand near the point of use; manufactured sand from crushed rock is the standard substitute. The crisis, on the combined record, is one of governance and local damage, not of the planet running out of sand.

4. The Carbon Ledger: The Emissions Are the Chemistry

Cement's share of global carbon dioxide emissions is 7 to 8 percent, the IEA carrying the lower figure and recent peer-reviewed reviews the higher, and the composition of that share is the finding that governs everything else in this section. Roughly 60 percent of cement's emissions are process emissions: the CO2 driven out of limestone when it is calcined into clinker, released by the reaction itself before any fuel is burned. The remaining 40 percent is energy. The consequence is arithmetic, not opinion: a cement works running entirely on clean electricity still emits the majority of its current footprint, because the footprint is the product. This is why cement is the industrial sector least amenable to the standard decarbonization story, and why the credible fixes are the ones that change the chemistry or catch the gas.

Two of the three fixes are in commerce in 2025 and 2026; the third is in press releases, and the desk prints them at their true sizes. Clinker substitution is the oldest lever, replacing part of the clinker with other binders, and its current form is LC3, a cement built on calcined clay and limestone: standardized in India as IS 18189 in 2023, in commercial production at JK Cement's Mangrol works from July 2025, poured at scale at Noida International Airport that September, and produced by CBI Ghana's flash-calcination plant from May 2025. Capture is the second: Heidelberg Materials' Brevik plant in Norway, inaugurated June 18, 2025, is the world's first industrial-scale carbon capture facility at a cement works, designed to take about 400,000 tonnes of CO2 a year, roughly half the plant's emissions, for storage under the seabed by Northern Lights, heavily supported by the Norwegian state; a January 2026 trade report put its achieved capture rate at about 50 percent, limited by available waste heat, and its product sells as a zero-carbon cement at a premium. The third fix, electrochemical cement, is real as chemistry and absent as industry: Sublime Systems' product carries an ASTM performance designation from 2023, and Microsoft and Meta have signed offtake agreements, Meta's reported on November 12, 2026. Its first commercial plant, at Holyoke, Massachusetts, is unbuilt: the Energy Department cancelled its $87 million grant in May 2025, deployment is paused, and the company's target has slipped to about 2028. A November 2026 report that prints electrochemical cement as an operating alternative is printing a prospectus. The industry's own roadmap, from the IEA and the Global Cement and Concrete Association, leans on exactly the levers the record shows working: substitution, efficiency, and capture, in that order of present reality.

5. The Concrete Club: The Cartel in the Court Record

The most colorful claim in this file is also one of the best documented, because it was tried in federal court, and the court's version corrects the retellings in two particulars. In the 1980s, Manhattan concrete contracting above a threshold was allocated, not bid. The controlling account is the Second Circuit's in United States v. Scopo and Montemarano, 861 F.2d 339: concrete contracts over $2 million were controlled by a club of six contractors, coordinated by four crime families (the supplied summaries say five; the appellate record says four), whose members paid Ralph Scopo 2 percent of the contract price, the cut divided among the four families. Contracts at or below $2 million were a separate Colombo-family extortion documented in the same record. Scopo was the scheme's hinge: a Colombo soldier who was also, from 1977 to April 1985, president of the Cement and Concrete Workers District Council, holding both the cartel's enforcement and the union's labor supply in one pair of hands. The leverage was the material itself: a perishable product, on a 90-minute clock, delivered by union drivers to sites that could not pause, meant a slowdown or a missing truck could destroy a pour and its contractor with it, a point Owen's account makes and the trial record supports.

The ending is a matter of sentence. Scopo was convicted in the Mafia Commission Trial, the government's case against the Commission of La Cosa Nostra; the jury convicted on November 19, 1986, and on January 13, 1987, Scopo was sentenced to 100 years in prison and a $240,000 fine. He died in federal custody on March 9, 1993. The supplied material attributes vivid quoted dialogue to a prosecutor, Peter Lieb; Lieb is documented as a real organized-crime prosecutor in the Southern District in that period, and the desk could verify neither the quotes nor their setting in any source, so they are not printed. What the record carries without assistance is sufficient: a two-percent tax on the material a city is built from, collected for years, ended by a racketeering trial and a sentence measured in centuries. New York, on Owen's figure, poured a Hoover Dam's worth of concrete every eighteen months through the years the club operated; printed as Owen's, the figure gives the cartel's tax base its scale.

6. The Culture File: Owen, a Talk Piece, a Memoir, and a Movie

The material's literature is thin and strong, and its standard was set on November 10, 2003. David Owen's “Concrete Jungle,” published in that issue of The New Yorker under the subtitle “Giant wrecking balls, Mob contracts, and the cement that holds the city together,” is the magazine's fact piece in its classic form: an overlooked substance under the reader's feet, unfolded into chemistry, engineering, history, demolition, and crime, and closed on the cycle of a city grinding itself down and pouring itself back up. Its reporting on the Concrete Club is corroborated by the court record in section 5, with the family's count corrected. Its scale figures, the Hoover Dam equivalence for New York's pours and the 40,000 psi strength, are printed in this report as Owen's, because the article is paywalled and no primary source carries them independently; the piece's reputation rests on the parts that check. The magazine returned to the material in smaller forms. Lauren Collins's “Rising,” dated June 7, 2010, is a Talk of the Town piece, not the feature the supplied summaries describe; its opening is the record of a morning: “Every morning at four-thirty, sixty concrete trucks, from Brooklyn, from Queens, from New Jersey,” converging on the World Trade Center site as One World Trade Center climbed past its twentieth floor. And the magazine's Personal History, “Impalpable Dust,” of March 27, 1989, belongs to the file properly: M. R. Montgomery, the Boston Globe columnist, writing about his father, an engineer on the Fort Peck Dam, a piece later carried into his memoir Saying Goodbye. One of the supplied summaries credits the piece to Roger Angell; the magazine's own archive says Montgomery, and the error is printed here because correcting the byline of the literature is part of reporting the literature.

The current entry is a film, and it is the strangest document in the file. John Wilson's The History of Concrete, his first feature after his HBO series How To with John Wilson ended in 2023, premiered at Sundance on January 22, 2026, and opened in limited American release through Magnolia Pictures on September 18, 2026; it was still screening in November. Its premise is on the record and requires no embellishment: unable to finance a documentary about concrete on the subject's merits, Wilson attended a workshop on the Hallmark television-movie formula during the Writers Guild strike and built the documentary inside that formula, commercial beats and all, a structure that reviewers, including The New Yorker's Richard Brody, who called the result pointedly and urgently political, have treated as the film's method rather than its gimmick. The film ranges as its director's series ranged, from a crack in his own house's foundation to a Las Vegas concrete trade show, sidewalk gum removal, and a 3,100-mile footrace in Queens. The desk's finding on the culture file is the one the three decades of it support: the material defeats ordinary treatment. Owen mastered it with reporting, Montgomery with a father's biography, Wilson by surrendering to a borrowed plot. Every treatment is an attempt to make a reader or a viewer look at the gray surface under everything and see it. The record says they keep succeeding, briefly, one work at a generation, and the surface closes over again.

Sources and Method

Principal sources: USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, cement chapter, read directly, and MCS 2026 figures as reported; Vaclav Smil, Making the Modern World, and the Washington Post's March 24, 2015 account quoting USGS specialist Hendrik van Oss; Seymour, Masic et al., “Hot mixing,” Science Advances 9(1), January 6, 2023; Vaserman, Masic et al., “An unfinished Pompeian construction site reveals ancient Roman building technology,” Nature Communications 16:10847, December 9, 2025; Encyclopaedia Britannica on Portland cement, Aspdin (British Patent 5022, 1824), Monier, and Hennebique, with Lambot (1848/1855) and Wilkinson (1854) from the historical record; US Bureau of Reclamation, Hoover Dam FAQ; ASTM C94's discharge-time requirement (1935–2021) from standards histories; RSC Sustainability (2025) review and IEA figures for the 7–8 percent emissions share and the 60/40 process-energy split; Heidelberg Materials and Longship reporting on Brevik (inaugurated June 18, 2025) and January 2026 trade reporting on achieved capture; LC3 records (IS 18189:2023; JK Cement, July 2025; CBI Ghana, May 2025); Data Center Dynamics (May 29, 2026) and trade reporting (November 12, 2026) on Sublime Systems; United States v. Scopo and Montemarano, 861 F.2d 339 (2d Cir. 1988), and the Commission Trial sentencing record (January 13, 1987); UN Environment Programme sand reports (April 26, 2022; May 2026) and the USGS position on sand resources; The New Yorker's own pages for Owen (November 10, 2003), Collins (June 7, 2010), Montgomery (March 27, 1989), and its September 2026 coverage of Wilson; Sundance and Magnolia Pictures records for the film. Corrections to the material supplied to the desk: the Concrete Club was coordinated by four families, not five, and the threshold in the appellate record is $2 million, not $5 million; the 4.1-billion-tonne cement figure is 2023's, superseded by a declining series; “Impalpable Dust” is M. R. Montgomery's, not Roger Angell's; Collins's “Rising” is a Talk of the Town piece, not a feature; quoted dialogue attributed to prosecutor Peter Lieb could not be verified and is excluded, Lieb himself being documented; the Wilson film's runtime is listed at 101 minutes by one review and 102 by another, and the report prints neither. Figures stated by Owen are attributed to Owen. Research files for this report are retained by the desk.

### Podcasting: What the Record Shows About Who Invented It, Who Named It, and Who Made It Famous

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-13T17:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-13-podcasting-record.html

Special Report

Podcasting · Adam Curry · Dave Winer · RSS · The Comedy Wave · Podcasting 2.0

Objective

Podcasting: What the Record Shows About Who Invented It, Who Named It, and Who Made It Famous

Podcasting was invented between 2000 and 2005 by at least seven people in four countries: a developer who proposed attaching media to a syndication feed, the engineer who built the attachment and wrote down, at the time, whose persistence had produced it, a journalist who made the first content for it, an engineer who closed the last gap to the portable player, two men who named it independently, and a former MTV host who supplied the use case, the prototype software, the test feed, and twenty years of evangelism. The popular story gives the invention to the comedians who arrived in 2009 and made the medium famous, and gives the former MTV host either too little credit, as a haircut with a microphone, or too much, as a lone inventor. This report prints the dated documents and lets the credit fall where they put it.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1700 ET, Friday, November 13, 2026.

The File in Brief

Podcasting's mechanism was working before it had a name, its name existed before most of its famous hosts had recorded anything, and its mass market opened on June 28, 2005, when Apple put more than 3,000 shows into iTunes and took a million subscriptions in two days, four years before Adam Carolla, Marc Maron, and Joe Rogan launched the shows the popular story starts with. The mechanism is one element in a syndication format: the RSS enclosure, proposed by Tristan Louis in October 2000, implemented by Dave Winer in the RSS 0.92 specification of December 25, 2000, and demonstrated by Winer on January 11, 2001, in an essay, “Payloads for RSS,” that credits Adam Curry's persistence as what got it built. The first sustained original content arrived in September 2003, Christopher Lydon's interview feed, built by Winer; Kevin Marks demonstrated delivery from feed to iPod in October 2003; Ben Hammersley put the word podcasting in print in February 2004 and Dannie Gregoire gave the practice its working name that September; Curry's Daily Source Code, from August 13, 2004, was the developer community's test feed and the medium's first celebrity-fronted show. Curry himself was not the mascot of the story but one of its principals: an MTV host who registered mtv.com in 1993 and fought his network over it in federal court, then co-founded a web company absorbed into a public company in a 1999 merger the SEC records at a reported $230 million valuation, though what he personally took from it is documented nowhere, and his own later figure for it is his own. The comedians' contribution is real and different in kind: Carolla proved a fired radio host could rebuild an audience independently, Maron built the confessional interview into the medium's prestige form, Rogan built its largest audience and its licensing price, and none of the three invented, or claimed to invent, the machinery. The record also corrects the record-keepers: the first download record belongs to Ricky Gervais's newspaper show in 2006, Carolla's 2011 Guinness title is a certification his own certified total contradicts against Gervais's published numbers, and the Library of Congress introduces Curry as the Podfather in a sentence that misdates his show by a year. The argument the inventors started, over whether the medium stays open, is still running: it is called Podcasting 2.0, and its founding show, Curry and John C. Dvorak's No Agenda, ended on October 29, 2026, three months after Dvorak's death, after nineteen years.

The desk's method is the paper's method. Material was supplied to the desk as a stack of AI-assistant summaries. Every checkable claim was re-verified against the primary record before printing: Winer's own essays and the RSS specification, the federal court opinion in MTV Networks v. Curry, SEC filings for the THINK New Ideas merger, Apple’s press releases of June 2005 and March 2024, the Guinness certifications as reported contemporaneously, the court record of the Personal Audio settlement, the transcript of Rogan's March 4, 2020 interview with Curry, and the Podcast Index's own statistics. The supplied material was unusually accurate in outline and repeatedly wrong in load-bearing detail; the corrections are printed in the body where they belong, including three against the legend of Curry himself and one against the Library of Congress.

1. The VJ Was an Engineer: Curry Before Podcasting

The popular dismissal of Adam Curry rests on his first job, and his first job is the least informative part of his record. Curry hosted MTV's Headbangers Ball and Top 20 Video Countdown from 1987; his written contract ran to May 1992 and he continued on informal terms until April 1994. In the spring of 1993, while still on air, he registered mtv.com with InterNIC and began running it himself, announcing the address on MTV broadcasts that August, because the network's executives had no internet presence and no plan for one. The network's formal demand that he stop came on January 19, 1994, while he was still its host; he resigned that April; MTV sued on May 5, 1994. His own announcement of the suit survives, posted at 3:44 in the morning of May 10, 1994, to the Interesting People mailing list, signed adam@mtv.com, under the subject line “MTV SUES CURRY.” The case, MTV Networks v. Curry, 867 F. Supp. 202, reached one reported decision: on October 28, 1994, Judge McKenna denied MTV's motion to dismiss Curry's counterclaims, a ruling that recited allegations and decided nothing about who owned the domain. No court ever decided it. The parties settled on March 24, 1995, on undisclosed terms; MTV took mtv.com, and Curry kept metaverse.com. A settlement figure of $100,000 circulates in later retellings; the desk found no source for it in the case record, and does not print it as fact.

What he did next is a matter of securities filings, and the filings support the entrepreneur and not the fortune. Curry co-founded OnRamp, an early web design and hosting firm, which was rolled into THINK New Ideas, a NASDAQ-listed interactive agency where contemporary coverage identifies him as chief technology officer. SEC records document THINK's merger into AnswerThink Consulting Group on November 5, 1999, at a 0.70 exchange ratio with roughly 7.55 million shares issued; contemporary trade coverage valued the transaction at $230 million, and Curry appears in the filings as a THINK director holding options, and as a signatory to the merger agreement. No filing the desk found states what Curry personally realized, and the figure that circulates, his own statement on a 2026 episode of No Agenda that he left with “maybe $2 million,” is a self-reported number repeated by net-worth websites that cite no audit and may be echoing him. The desk prints the supportable version: by 2000, the former VJ had run a web company into a public-company merger and was living on the proceeds and the obsession together. Wired's March 2005 profile opens with his own summary of the double life, verbatim: “I've always had this total dual life as a geek and a celebrity.” That profile matters again in section 7, because it also contains two factual errors that hardened into the popular story.

2. The Mechanism: One Tag, and the Essay That Assigns the Credit

Podcasting is a solution to a delivery problem, and the problem is dated. In 2000, connections were increasingly always-on and still slow: a click on a media file meant a wait, and streaming meant a stutter. The idea that solved it was to let the computer do the waiting: a subscription program would check a publisher's feed overnight, download new media files in the background, and have them ready on a portable player in the morning. Audio files could already be posted to websites; what did not exist was the subscription, the machine-readable announcement that a new file existed and where it lived. On October 13, 2000, on the syndication mailing list, developer Tristan Louis proposed exactly that: an addition to the RSS 0.92 specification letting a feed item carry sound and video attachments. Dave Winer, the format's steward and the author of the blogging tools Frontier and Radio UserLand, implemented the proposal in somewhat different form as the enclosure element: three attributes, a file's URL, its length in bytes, and its media type. The element entered the RSS 0.92 specification on December 25, 2000.

The strongest credit document in the entire record is Winer's own demonstration essay, written at the time, before there was anything to fight over. On January 11, 2001, in “Payloads for RSS,” Winer attached a Grateful Dead track, “Touch of Grey,” to a daily-song feed as the working example, described his system configured to download enclosures between 1 and 4 in the morning, and explained whose idea he had been resisting. The essay credits its teachers in its own text, “a mix of Marc, Adam and me,” naming Marc Canter and Adam Curry, and of Curry it says, verbatim: “When I started talking with Adam late last year, he wanted me to think about high quality video&hellip; But Adam persisted and showed me that if I was willing to change my point of view, it could work, without any waiting and with very high quality.” Curry's own dated posts from October 2000 press the same case, and Winer's Scripting News answered them the same month; the specific New York hotel meeting of the retellings rests on the participants' later accounts, which Curry was still not correcting when an interviewer put it to him in 2020, and the desk prints the meeting as their consistent account and the October documents as the hard record. The division the essay documents is the division this report uses: Curry supplied the use case and the persistence; Winer built the mechanism. Neither man, in 2001, claimed the other's half.

3. Content, the Last Gap, and the Name: 2003–2004

For two years the enclosure was a mechanism in search of a medium, and the medium arrived as journalism. Winer spent 2003 and 2004 as a fellow at Harvard's Berkman Center, where the veteran broadcaster Christopher Lydon was a colleague. Lydon began posting interviews as blog entries with audio links in July 2003, and his first interviewee was Winer himself, who later said the first podcast in human history was the interview he recorded with Lydon that month. It was not yet a podcast in the mechanical sense: the audio sat behind manual links. In September 2003, Winer built Lydon's blog a special RSS feed with enclosures, and from that month the interviews arrived by subscription, downloaded automatically: the first sustained original spoken-word podcast feed on the record. The same summer, educator Stephen Downes demonstrated Ed Radio, which aggregated and syndicated MP3 audio, evidence that the idea was converging from several directions at once. The last gap was the player. At BloggerCon, held at Harvard on October 4 and 5, 2003, Kevin Marks, an Apple engineer until that year, demonstrated in public a script that took enclosure files from a feed, passed them through iTunes, and put them on an iPod. Curry and Marks discussed collaborating afterward, and Curry's own RSS-to-iPod prototype post is dated October 12, 2003. By the end of 2003, every element of podcasting existed: the tag, the feed, the content, and the pipe to the pocket.

What it lacked was a word, and the word arrived twice. On February 12, 2004, Ben Hammersley's Guardian column on Lydon's work asked, of the new form: “But what to call it? Audioblogging? Podcasting? GuerillaMedia?” That is the first located print use of podcasting, floated as one of three candidates. Seven months later, on September 15, 2004, Dannie J. Gregoire proposed podcasting and podcaster on the ipodder-dev mailing list and registered podcaster.net the next day; Dave Slusher used the word on a podcast on September 18. Gregoire states he had not seen Hammersley's article; independent coinage can be neither proved nor disproved, and the desk prints it as his statement. The verdict of the two men with the most at stake in the question is on the record and agrees: Winer writes that “Dannie Gregoire really named what we were doing,” and Curry said the same to Rogan in 2020. In 2005, podcast was the New Oxford American Dictionary's Word of the Year. The name, like the medium, is a multi-party artifact.

4. The Show, the Software, and the Store: 2004–2005

The Daily Source Code was infrastructure wearing a show's clothes. Curry's AppleScript for moving enclosures to an iPod, a hack in the RSS2iPod line he had prototyped in October 2003, was released openly in August 2004 under the name iPodder, and on August 13, 2004, Curry launched the Daily Source Code explicitly as a live feed developers could test their downloading clients against. It ran 867 episodes to November 30, 2013, and functioned as the new medium's workshop and bulletin board: new shows were announced on it, new clients were debugged against it, and its host, a former MTV star with a broadcaster's instincts, made the test feed a program people listened to for itself. The division of labor on the software deserves print precision, supplied at the time by Rogers Cadenhead, who served with Curry on the RSS Advisory Board: Curry “released an Applescript hack as open source that led to the first standalone podcasting client. But he was never a developer on iPodder (now known as Juice).” The standalone client the world used was built by the open-source project's developers, later renamed Juice partly under Apple trademark pressure over the name. Curry's contribution was the prototype, the test feed, the audience, and the promotion; the engineering of the application belongs to the developers, and the record supports exactly that and no more.

The business and the mass market arrived together, and both predate the popular story's start. PodShow, the podcast network Curry co-founded with Ron Bloom in San Francisco, was incorporated on October 1, 2004, not 2005 as the supplied summaries and most retellings have it; its public launch and first money belong to 2005, when Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia Capital, and Sherpalo invested about $8.85 million in August. The company, later renamed Mevio, raised $38.85 million in total and ceased operations in April 2014. In May 2005, Steve Jobs previewed podcast support in iTunes at the D3 conference, playing episode 180 of the Daily Source Code on stage. Apple's press release of June 28, 2005, put podcasting in iTunes 4.9 with a directory of more than 3,000 free shows, quoted Jobs calling podcasting “the next generation of radio,” and named Curry's show in its featured list; Apple's release of June 30 announced more than one million subscriptions in the first two days, a figure the desk prints as Apple's own. From June 2005, anyone with the world's dominant music software could subscribe to any show in the directory in two clicks. The invention period was over. Everything after is audience.

5. The Record Books: Gervais, Carolla, and a Patent

The first download record of the mass era belongs to a British newspaper's comedy show, and it is not close. The Ricky Gervais Show, produced with Stephen Merchant and Karl Pilkington and distributed by Guardian Unlimited, launched as a podcast on December 5, 2005. In February 2006, The Guardian reported Guinness World Records' ratification of the show as the most downloaded podcast, on an average of more than 261,000 downloads per episode in its first month and 2.9 million cumulative downloads in just over two months. The BBC put the show at nearly 18 million downloads by September 2006, and its total passed 300 million by March 2011. It was, structurally, a repurposed radio-format production from a national newspaper, closer to broadcast economics than to the garage model the popular story celebrates, and it held the record five years before the man the popular story calls the record-breaker.

Adam Carolla's 2011 Guinness title is real as a certification and false as a comparison, and the desk prints both halves. Carolla's terrestrial show ended with his station's format change; the final broadcast was February 20, 2009, and his podcast debuted February 23, 2009, drawing 250,000 downloads on its first day, proving at once that a fired radio host could rebuild his audience as an independent. In May 2011, Guinness certified The Adam Carolla Show as the most downloaded podcast, on 59,574,843 downloads from March 2009 to March 16, 2011. Gervais's show had passed 300 million downloads by that same March, roughly five times the certified figure. Guinness records are claimant-driven and fee-bearing; the 2011 certification measures who applied and paid, not who was largest. Carolla overtook Gervais in the book, not in downloads. The patent fight that followed deserves the same precision. In February 2013, Personal Audio LLC sued Carolla's company under a patent it claimed covered episodic online content delivery; Carolla crowdfunded his defense, raising more than $475,000, refused to settle on the troll's terms, and on August 15, 2014, the parties filed a joint dismissal under a confidential settlement in which no payment by Carolla appears in any record. The patent survived his case. What killed its asserted claims was a separate action: the Electronic Frontier Foundation's challenge at the Patent Office, which revoked five provisions in April 2015, with the Supreme Court declining review on May 14, 2018. Carolla fought and settled; the EFF invalidated. Both sentences are the record.

6. The Popularizers at Their True Size: 2009–2014

Marc Maron's contribution is a form, and he has never claimed it was more. WTF with Marc Maron launched September 1, 2009, after the cancellation of his Air America program, with comedian Jeff Ross as first guest; the early episodes were recorded in Air America's New York studios with Maron's retained keycard, and the famous garage came later, in Los Angeles. On June 22, 2015, episode 613 carried a sitting president, Barack Obama, interviewed in that garage. The show's final episode, number 1,686, was released October 13, 2025, with Obama returning as the last guest. The desk found no statement by Maron claiming to have invented podcasting. What he built, starting seven years after Lydon's feed, was the long confessional interview as the medium's prestige genre; the popular story's error is not honoring him, it is starting the clock with him.

Joe Rogan's contribution is scale, and the scale is documented in money and in one transcript that corrects the legend better than any history has. The Joe Rogan Experience was first recorded on December 24, 2009, as a live Ustream broadcast with comedian Brian Redban. Spotify's exclusive licensing deal, announced May 19, 2020, was reported by the Wall Street Journal at more than $100 million; reporting in February 2022 put the actual figure at $200 million over three years, and the figures are press-reported estimates, since Spotify has disclosed none of them. The February 2024 renewal, reported at up to $250 million, ended the exclusivity and returned the show to wide distribution. On March 4, 2020, in episode 1436, Rogan hosted Adam Curry and opened the credit exchange himself: “You're the guy who made the very first podcast. You even came up with the name of it, right?” Curry corrected him on air: “I didn't come up with the name.” Curry credited Hammersley's earlier print use, said “Dannie Gregoire really named what we were doing,” dated the technology to 2000, described building on Winer's RSS work, and added, of the honorific itself: “I didn't name myself the podfather, but people started calling me that.” The legend and the man's own testimony differ, and the testimony matches the documents.

Serial belongs in the record as a separate event, not a chapter of the comedy story. Serial, a This American Life spinoff hosted by Sarah Koenig, debuted October 3, 2014, reinvestigating a 1999 murder across twelve weekly episodes. On November 18, 2014, Apple announced it was the fastest podcast ever to reach 5 million downloads and streams on iTunes, a figure the desk prints as Apple's; season one passed 68 million downloads by February 2015 and won a Peabody Award. The New York Times called it podcasting's first breakout hit, defensible only with breakout doing the work, since Gervais and Carolla had drawn larger numbers inside a smaller medium. What Serial proved, a decade after the invention, was that serialized journalism built for the form could hold a mass audience to a schedule, which is a different discovery from the comedians': theirs was that independence paid; Serial's was that the feed could carry narrative weight.

7. The Credit War, and How the Legend Got Typeset

The ugliest documented episode in the record is also the most instructive, because it is the invention's participants editing the invention. Four times in 2005, edits to Wikipedia's podcasting article were made from an IP address registered to Adam Curry. On February 5, 2005, the address removed a sentence crediting Stephen Downes with distributing MP3 audio over RSS and rewrote Curry's own role to read that podcasting “was developed thanks to Adam Curry's original iPodder script and the success it fostered.” On November 3, 2005, it removed the sentence crediting Kevin Marks with the BloggerCon demonstration. Marks traced the address; Rogers Cadenhead documented the pattern that December. Curry acknowledged the edits and apologized to Marks, saying he had meant to rewrite the paragraph from his own recollection. The desk prints the fairness note the episode requires: Cadenhead was a Winer collaborator, served with Curry on the RSS Advisory Board, and disclosed his position in his own piece; his factual core, the edit diffs and the address registration, checks out independently. Winer, for his part, had publicly objected that May to a Wired News interview billing Curry as podcasting's inventor, and each man accused the other of being written out of the history. The documentary irony is the finding: the January 2001 essay, written before the money and the fame, divides the credit more fairly than either participant's later editing, which is why this report rests on it.

The legend was typeset by institutions, and the institutions' errors are still standing. Wired's March 2005 profile of Curry contains the geek-and-celebrity self-description quoted in section 1, and then states, verbatim, that “Curry's show, The Daily Source Code, was the first ever podcast.” It was not; Lydon's enclosure feed predates it by a year. The same profile places Curry's conversion to audio at “BloggerCon in 2001”; BloggerCon did not exist until October 2003. The Library of Congress now hosts an interview with Curry on its National Recording Preservation Plan pages and introduces him with the honor and the error fused in one sentence: “Adam Curry began his pioneering podcast 'Daily Source Code' in 2003 and has remained a fixture of the medium ever since. This is an interview with the man known as 'The Podfather.'” The show began in August 2004; 2003 is Lydon's year. The sentence is the popular history in miniature, and correcting it, in one place, with the documents open, is what this report is for.

8. The Second Act: No Agenda and Podcasting 2.0

The bridge between the invention and its defense is one show, and the show has now ended. No Agenda debuted October 26, 2007, co-hosted by Curry and John C. Dvorak, twice weekly, carrying no advertising from its first episode and funded entirely by listeners under the model its hosts named value for value, years before that model had machinery. It ran nineteen years and roughly 1,900 episodes. Dvorak recorded his last episode on July 19, 2026, and died the following day; Curry closed the show with a final episode on October 29, 2026. The desk states the fact plainly because it belongs to the record this report covers: the program that carried the open medium's economics in practice, hosted by one of its inventors and the dean of its commentators, is complete.

Podcasting 2.0 is the same argument Curry and Winer started in 2000, resumed against new gatekeepers. In September 2020, Curry and developer Dave Jones launched the Podcast Index, an open directory and programming interface for every podcast feed, free for any use, built explicitly as an alternative to directories controlled by Apple and Spotify, through which most listening then flowed. Around it grew the Podcasting 2.0 initiative: a podcast namespace of more than thirty new RSS tags that add, to any open feed, the features closed platforms had used to justify their gardens, transcripts, chapters, live streaming alerts, person credits, soundbites, cross-application comments, alternate audio and video versions, and a value tag carrying Lightning Network payment details, so listeners can stream satoshis to a host by the minute or send a payment with a message attached, a boostagram. Its notification system, Podping, writes publication notices to a public blockchain so applications learn of new episodes in seconds rather than polling feeds; major independent hosts send podpings, and the largest platforms mostly do not. The Index's own statistics, read in September 2026, report 4,728,565 feeds indexed and about 167 million episodes; the same statistics report 472,076 feeds with a new episode in the prior 90 days, about one feed in ten still publishing, and the desk prints both numbers because the first without the second inflates the living medium by an order of magnitude. Adoption is real and partial: independent hosts including Blubrry, Captivate, and RSS.com document tag support; listening applications including Fountain, Podverse, and TrueFans support namespace features and the payment layer; Apple adopted the namespace's transcript tag in March 2024, on its own terms, while its chapters support arrived only in late 2025, after years of ignoring the chapters tag, and no major platform implements the whole namespace. The payment economy remains small; on the Podcasting 2.0 program itself in October 2026, a supporting application's founder reported streaming-payment volume had fallen to near zero that July. And one correction the summaries consistently garble: Podcasting 2.0 issues no certification; the PSP-1 certification mark belongs to a separate body, the Podcast Standards Project. The mechanism is specified, implemented, and open. Its economy is a beginning, and its founders' claim for it is not scale but custody: an index no company can close is the 2000 argument, that the feed belongs to whoever publishes it, restated for the platform era.
